## Proof

We evaluate

$$I = \lim_{n\to\infty}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{\cos nx}{x+1}\,dx.$$

**Claim.** $I = 0$.

The key tool is the **Riemann–Lebesgue lemma**: if $f\in L^1([a,b])$ is Lebesgue integrable on a finite interval $[a,b]$, then

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_a^b f(x)\cos(nx)\,dx = 0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \lim_{n\to\infty}\int_a^b f(x)\sin(nx)\,dx = 0.$$

We verify the hypotheses. Define $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x+1}$ on $[0,2\pi]$.

- The denominator $x+1$ satisfies $x+1 \in [1, 2\pi+1]$ on $[0,2\pi]$, so $x+1\geq 1 > 0$ throughout; $f$ is continuous on $[0,2\pi]$.
- Being continuous on a compact interval, $f$ is bounded: $|f(x)|\leq 1$ for all $x\in[0,2\pi]$.
- Hence $f\in L^1([0,2\pi])$, with $\int_0^{2\pi}|f(x)|\,dx = \ln(2\pi+1) < \infty$.

All hypotheses of the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma are satisfied. Applying it with $a=0$, $b=2\pi$, and $f(x)=\frac{1}{x+1}$,

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{\cos nx}{x+1}\,dx = 0.$$

Therefore $I = 0$.
